fact: Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart.

Butterflies taste with their feet.

Hedgehogs are immune to a lot of snake venom.
Koalas have fingerprints almost indistinguishable from human ones.
Owls can rotate their necks up to 270 degrees.
African grey parrots can understand numerical concepts, not just mimic speech.

Ants can carry objects up to 50 times their own body weight.

Snakes smell using their tongues, which pick up particles and pass them to the Jacobson's organ.

Spider silk is, by weight, stronger than steel.

Lobsters taste using their legs.
The mantis shrimp can punch with the acceleration of a bullet, fast enough to boil water around its claw.
Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time so they can keep breathing and watch for predators.
A walrus can slow its heart rate to withstand the cold pressure of deep dives.
Humpback whale songs can travel for miles underwater and change from year to year.
A narwhal's tusk is actually an elongated tooth packed with millions of nerve endings.
Alligators can go through thousands of teeth in a lifetime, regrowing each one that falls out.
A bald eagle's eyesight is about four to five times sharper than a human's.
A duck's quack technically does echo, contrary to the old myth.
Swans can fly at altitudes of over 8,000 meters during migration.
Chickens can remember and recognize over 100 different faces, including humans.
A turkey's snood, the fleshy bit above its beak, changes color depending on its mood.

Sparrows take dust baths to help remove parasites from their feathers.
The kiwi bird lays an egg that can be up to 20% of its own body weight.
Crows can recognize individual human faces and hold grudges for years.

An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.
African elephants can detect rainfall from over 100 miles away.
A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the same protein found in human hair and nails.
Hippos secrete a natural reddish oily substance that acts as sunscreen and an antiseptic.
Every zebra's stripe pattern is unique, like a human fingerprint.
The okapi, despite its zebra-like stripes, is actually the closest living relative of the giraffe.
A cheetah can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in about three seconds.
A tiger's stripe pattern is unique to each individual, similar to a human fingerprint.
A lion's roar can be heard from as far as 8 kilometers away.
Leopards are strong enough to haul prey twice their own body weight up into trees.
Wolves have a much stronger sense of smell than dogs and can detect scents up to a mile away.
Foxes use Earth's magnetic field to help judge distance when hunting under snow.
A grizzly bear's bite force is strong enough to crush a bowling ball.
Polar bear fur is actually transparent, not white, and their skin underneath is black.
Giant pandas spend up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo.
Kangaroos cannot walk backward because of the shape of their tail and legs.
Wombats produce cube-shaped poop, which helps it stay stacked as a scent marker.
The platypus is one of the only mammals that lays eggs, and males can deliver venom through spurs on their hind legs.
A hamster's cheek pouches can stretch back to its shoulders when packed with food.
Mice can laugh, in the form of ultrasonic chirps, when tickled.
Rabbits can see almost 360 degrees around them without moving their heads.
A porcupine has around 30,000 quills, each of which can detach on contact.
A chipmunk can carry more than its own body volume of food in its cheek pouches.
Horses can sleep both lying down and standing up thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs.
Narwhal tusks were sold in medieval Europe as unicorn horns.
Goats have rectangular pupils, giving them a wide field of peripheral vision.
Sheep can recognize and remember the faces of up to 50 other sheep for years.
Cows have best friends and show signs of stress when separated from them.
Pigs are among the most intelligent domesticated animals, able to learn tasks faster than dogs.
A dog's sense of smell is estimated to be tens of thousands of times more sensitive than a human's.
Cats can't taste sweetness because they lack the taste receptor gene for it.
Some field mice can survive falls from great heights because of their small mass and terminal velocity.
Wolverines can crush frozen bone and meat with jaws powerful enough to open frozen carcasses.
A deer's antlers are the fastest-growing bone tissue known, regrowing fully each year.
Wild boars have an excellent sense of smell and can detect food buried nearly a meter underground.

Llamas hum to communicate a range of emotions, from curiosity to distress.
Dromedary camels can drink over 100 liters of water in under 10 minutes.
Algae grows in a sloth's fur, giving it a greenish tint that helps it camouflage.
Capuchin monkeys have been observed using stone tools to crack open nuts.
Gorillas share about 98% of their DNA with humans.
Japanese macaques are known to bathe in hot springs to stay warm in winter.
Orangutans build a new sleeping nest out of branches and leaves almost every single night.
Raccoons have highly sensitive front paws and often appear to 'wash' food before eating it.
A skunk can accurately spray its defensive musk up to 3 meters.

Hares are born fully furred with open eyes, unlike rabbits which are born blind and hairless.
Rats are ticklish and will make ultrasonic chirping sounds similar to laughter when tickled.

Macaws can live for 50 to 60 years, sometimes outliving their human owners.

Pigeons can be trained to distinguish between different human artists' paintings.

Adelie penguins build nests out of small stones, and males often steal stones from their neighbors.
Flamingos can sleep while standing on one leg by locking a joint in place.
Sperm whales have the largest brain of any animal on Earth, weighing around 8 kilograms.
Orcas, also called killer whales, are actually the largest members of the dolphin family.
Great white sharks can detect a single drop of blood in about 100 liters of water.
The mimic octopus can impersonate the shape and movement of over a dozen other sea creatures.

Lobsters can regenerate a lost claw or leg over the course of several molts.
Some crab species can regrow a lost claw within a year through molting.
The nautilus has changed very little in over 500 million years, earning it the nickname 'living fossil.'
Some jellyfish species are biologically immortal, able to revert back to a juvenile polyp stage.
A starfish can regenerate an entire lost arm, and in some species, a whole new starfish from just one arm.
All clownfish are born male and can change to female if the dominant female of their group dies.
Salmon can use Earth's magnetic field to navigate back to the exact river where they were born.
A hammerhead shark's wide-set eyes give it nearly 360-degree vertical vision.
The gharial has one of the narrowest snouts of any crocodilian, specialized for catching fish.
Chameleons change color mainly to communicate mood and temperature, not just to camouflage.
Some frogs can freeze solid in winter and thaw back to life in spring.
Poison dart frogs get their toxicity from their diet; captive-bred frogs raised on different food are not poisonous.
Komodo dragons can detect carrion from several kilometers away using their forked tongues.
Sea turtles can navigate thousands of kilometers back to the exact beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
Pythons can go for months without eating after consuming a very large meal.
A spitting cobra can accurately aim venom at the eyes of a threat from over 2 meters away.
Emperor scorpions can survive without food for up to a year by slowing their metabolism.
Tarantulas can flick urticating hairs from their abdomen as a defense against predators.
Inside a chrysalis, most of a caterpillar's body dissolves into a soup before reforming into a butterfly.
Male crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, a process called stridulation.
Leafcutter ants don't eat the leaves they cut; they use them to farm a fungus that they actually eat.
Bumblebees can fly in colder temperatures than most other bee species by shivering their flight muscles to warm up.
Only female mosquitoes bite; they need the protein in blood to develop their eggs.
Ladybugs release a foul-smelling yellow fluid from their leg joints when threatened.
Monarch butterflies migrate up to 4,800 kilometers, a journey no single butterfly completes alone across generations.
A garden snail has thousands of tiny teeth arranged on a ribbon-like structure called a radula.
Geckos can climb smooth glass thanks to microscopic hair structures on their toes that create molecular adhesion.
Asian elephants can distinguish human languages and even genders associated with past threats.
Male elephant seals can hold their breath for up to two hours while diving for food.
Emperor penguin fathers incubate their eggs on their feet through the Antarctic winter without eating for months.
Flamingos feed with their heads upside down, using their beaks to filter food from water and mud.
Bowhead whales may live over 200 years, making them among the longest-lived mammals on Earth.
Lesser hedgehog tenrecs can go into torpor for up to seven months a year to save energy.
Giant river otters can reach over 1.8 meters in length and are nicknamed 'river wolves.'
Badger setts can be hundreds of years old and passed down through generations.
Two-toed sloths have more neck vertebrae than most other mammals, allowing broad movement.
Tree kangaroos can leap up to 18 meters down to the ground from trees without injury.
Honey badgers have skin so thick and loose that they can twist around and bite a predator holding them.
Ferrets perform a erratic sidestepping dance called the 'weasel war dance' when excited.
Nutria have orange teeth due to iron enamel that prevents degradation from water.
Mongooses have specialized acetylcholine receptors that make them resistant to cobra venom.
Moonrats, or gymnures, give off a strong garlic-like odor to ward off predators.
Vampire bats will regurgitate blood to share with starving colony mates.
Pygmy hippos spend far more time on land in forests than their larger, water-dwelling relatives.
Grevy's zebras are the largest wild equid species and have narrow, closely spaced stripes.
Javan rhinos are among the rarest large mammals, with fewer than 80 individuals left in the wild.
Sumatran rhinos are the smallest rhino species and are covered in a coat of reddish hair.
Snow leopards use their long, thick tails for balance and wrap them around their face for warmth.
Jaguars have a bite force strong enough to pierce turtle shells and reptilian hides.
Clouded leopards have the longest canine teeth relative to body size of any living cat.
Black panthers are not a separate species; they are melanistic jaguars or leopards.
Servals have the longest legs relative to body size of any cat species, useful for jumping.
Caracals can leap over 3 meters into the air to catch birds mid-flight.
Margays can turn their hind feet 180 degrees, enabling them to run down trees headfirst.

A fennec fox's giant ears dissipate body heat and allow it to hear prey underground.
Arctic fox fur changes from brown in summer to white in winter for camouflage.
Bat-eared foxes use their oversized ears to listen for termites underground, which form most of their diet.
African wild dogs have a success rate of over 80% when hunting, far higher than lions.
Despite its name, the maned wolf is not a true wolf, but a unique South American canine.
Sun bears have an extraordinarily long tongue, up to 25 cm, used to extract honey from hives.
Sloth bears can close their nostrils voluntarily to keep dirt out while sucking up termites.
The spectacled bear is the only native bear species living in South America.
Leopard seals are apex predators in Antarctica, possessing long, sharp teeth for catching penguins.
Ribbon seals have bold, natural white stripes contrasting against dark fur.
Harbor seal whiskers can sense the wake of swimming fish long after the fish has passed.

The vaquita is the smallest and most endangered cetacean on Earth.
A narwhal's tusk is actually a left canine tooth that grows straight through its upper lip.
Belugas can change the shape of their forehead 'melon' to modulate their vocalizations.
Fin whales are known as the 'greyhounds of the sea' due to their fast swimming speeds.
Minke whales produce loud sound bursts called 'bioduck' noises underwater.

Harpy eagles have talons larger than a grizzly bear's claws, allowing them to lift sloths.

Blind screech owls often live in symbiosis with blind snakes, which eat parasites in the owl's nest.
Burrowing owls nest underground and mimic rattlesnake rattles to deter predators.
The kakapo is the world's only flightless, nocturnal, and heaviest parrot species.
Kea parrots are famous for their curiosity and opening backpacks or picking car rubber.
Palm cockatoos use sticks to drum rhythmically against hollow trees to mark territory.
Lyrebirds can accurately mimic complex sounds, including chainsaws, car alarms, and camera shutters.
Male bowerbirds decorate elaborate bowers with blue objects to attract potential mates.

Hoopoes secrete a foul fluid from their preen gland to deter predators from their nests.

Secretarybirds stamp on snakes with a kicking force equal to five times their body weight.

Gentoo penguins are the fastest underwater swimmers among birds, reaching 36 km/h.

Spectacled caimans can change their skin color tone slightly using pigment cells.
Frilled lizards erect a large neck ruff and run on two legs when frightened.

Basilisk lizards can run across water for short distances, giving them the nickname 'Jesus Christ lizard.'
The black mamba's mouth interior is jet black, which it displays as a threat signal.
The inland taipan has the most toxic venom of any land snake, though it is shy and reclusive.
Boomslangs are rear-fanged snakes whose venom causes severe internal bleeding.
Yellow-bellied sea snakes can absorb up to 33% of their oxygen needs through their skin underwater.
Galapagos tortoises can live for over 100 years and survive months without food or water.

The matamata turtle uses suction feeding to snap up fish by opening its mouth rapidly.

Wood frogs freeze solid during winter, stopping their heart, and thaw out alive in spring.
Surinam toad eggs hatch directly out of embedded pockets on the mother's back.
Male Darwin's frogs carry developing tadpoles inside their vocal sacs until they metamorphose.

Fire salamanders can spray neurotoxic skin secretions at potential threats.

Flying fish can glide above the ocean surface for over 200 meters using enlarged pectoral fins.

Mudskippers can walk on land using their pectoral fins and breathe through skin.

Male orchid bees collect aromatic compounds from orchids to create unique perfume concoctions for mating.
